atoms.text: You will hear five people talking about free public transport. First, read the statements. Then listen to the audio file and match each speaker (1 to 5) with one of the statements.
atoms.sound: You will hear five people talking about free public transport. First reed the statements. Then listen to the audio file and match each speaker with one of the statements.

instruction.sound: speaker 1 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m4_chirp'>Well, honestly, I think free public transport would change the daily life of students like me a lot. Many of us already struggle with rent, food, and books. If buses and trains were free, it would relieve a big financial burden. Plus, it might even motivate more young people to use sustainable transport instead of driving by car. Of course, the government would have to find the money somewhere, but investing in young people and the environment seems like a reasonable priority to me.</voice> speaker 2 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f4In_chirp'>I’m sceptical about this idea. Free services often sound attractive at first, but they usually come with hidden costs. If the government finances public transport, it means taxpayers like me will pay more, and that is not necessarily fair. Also, I worry about quality. When something is free, the level of service often declines: delays, overcrowded trains, less comfort. I would rather pay for a ticket and know the system is reliable and efficient than end up with something cheap but unpleasant.</voice> speaker 3 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f10Us_chirp'>For me, this is a matter of climate justice. Transport is one of the biggest sources of emissions, and free public transport would encourage a real shift away from cars. The government spends billions on roads and car subsidies every year, so why not redirect some of that money to buses and trains? It’s not just about convenience, it’s about protecting the planet and making sustainable choices accessible to everyone, regardless of income.</voice> speaker 4 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m9Us_chirp'>Well, I’ve lived long enough to see many political promises come and go. Free public transport sounds wonderful, but I wonder if it’s realistic. Our healthcare system is under pressure, schools need funding, and there are so many urgent issues. I fear that free transport might simply not be affordable in the long run. Personally, I’d appreciate cheaper tickets for young people and seniors, but I don’t think making everything free is a sensible solution.</voice> speaker 5 <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f14Au_chirp'>From the perspective of someone working in the system, I have mixed feelings. On the one hand, more passengers mean more relevance for our jobs. On the other hand, if the trains get overcrowded without enough investment in infrastructure, it will create chaos. Drivers, conductors, and service staff are already under pressure. If the government really wants free transport, it must also guarantee better funding for maintenance, more vehicles, and fair working conditions, otherwise the system will simply collapse.</voice>
